intro.why: SVMs are the cleanest example of convex optimisation, duality and kernels in ML. The same ideas (margins, hinge loss, kernels, KKT) reappear in kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes, metric learning and the theory of deep networks.

sections.title: Linear classifiers
sections.plain: sign(w·x + b); many separating lines exist.
sections.body: A linear classifier is $f(\mathbf x,\mathbf w,b)=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b)$: points with $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b>0$ are labelled $+1$, those with $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b<0$ are $-1$. For linearly separable data, infinitely many lines classify the training set perfectly: "any of these would be fine… but which is best?" The decision boundary is the hyperplane $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b=0$; $\mathbf w$ is normal to it.

sections.title: Maximum margin and the linear SVM
sections.plain: Choose the separator with the widest empty band.
sections.body: The margin is the width the boundary could be widened before hitting a data point. Reasons to maximise it: (1) if the hyperplane passes close to training points, new data lying near training examples of the correct class may fall on the wrong side; (2) the solution is to maximise the margin. The maximum-margin linear classifier is the simplest SVM, the linear SVM (LSVM). Large-margin classifiers are also motivated by statistical learning theory: the VC-dimension bound for margin-$\rho$ hyperplanes on data of radius $R$ scales with $R^2/\rho^2$, independent of input dimension.

sections.title: Support vectors
sections.plain: The points on the margin determine everything.
sections.body: Geometrically, the max-margin hyperplane is completely determined by the points nearest to it. Points lying on the margin are the support vectors: the points which, if removed, would alter the position of the dividing hyperplane. All other points can move (without crossing the margin) or be deleted without changing the solution.

sections.title: Margin width mathematically
sections.plain: Canonical scaling makes the margin 2/‖w‖.
sections.body:
Because $(\mathbf w,b)$ and $(c\mathbf w,cb)$ describe the same hyperplane, fix the scale so that the closest points satisfy:

$$\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x^++b=+1,\qquad \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x^-+b=-1.$$

The margin is the projection of $\mathbf x^+-\mathbf x^-$ onto the unit normal $\mathbf w/\|\mathbf w\|$:

$$M=(\mathbf x^+-\mathbf x^-)\cdot\frac{\mathbf w}{\|\mathbf w\|}=\frac{\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x^+-\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x^-}{\|\mathbf w\|}=\frac{(1-b)-(-1-b)}{\|\mathbf w\|}=\frac{2}{\|\mathbf w\|}.$$

Maximising $M=2/\|\mathbf w\|$ is equivalent to minimising $\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2$, which is smooth and convex. The distance of any point to the boundary is $|\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b|/\|\mathbf w\|$.

sections.title: The hard-margin primal problem
sections.plain: Quadratic objective, linear inequality constraints.
sections.body:
Find $\mathbf w,b$ such that

$$\Phi(\mathbf w)=\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2\ \text{is minimised, subject to}\ y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1\ \ \forall i.$$

The single constraint combines the two cases: for $y_i=+1$, $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b\ge1$; for $y_i=-1$, $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b\le-1$. This is a quadratic program (quadratic objective, all constraints linear), a well-studied class with many solvers. The solution introduces a Lagrange multiplier $\alpha_i$ for every constraint:

$$L(\mathbf w,b,\boldsymbol\alpha)=\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2-\sum_i\alpha_i\left[y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)-1\right],\quad\alpha_i\ge0.$$

sections.title: Constrained optimisation basics
sections.plain: Objective, constraints, feasible and optimal solutions.
sections.body:
General form: minimise $f(\mathbf x)$ subject to $g_i(\mathbf x)=0,\ i=1..p$ (equality) and $h_i(\mathbf x)\le0,\ i=1..m$ (inequality). $f$ is the objective; the value $\mathbf x^*$ found must respect all constraints.

ProblemSolution
min $x^2$$x^*=0$
min $x^2$ s.t. $x=1$$x^*=1$ (only feasible point)
min $x^2$ s.t. $x\ge1$$x^*=1$ (constraint active)
min $x^2$ s.t. $x=1,\ x<0$infeasible (empty feasible set)

Definitions: a solution assigns values to variables; a feasible solution satisfies all constraints; the objective value is $f$ at that solution; an optimal solution (minimisation) has objective value ≤ that of every other feasible solution.

sections.title: Lagrange multipliers and the worked example
sections.plain: At the optimum ∇f = λ∇g.
sections.body:
A constrained problem is rewritten as a Lagrange function using multipliers. For maximise $f(x,y)=x^2y$ subject to $g:\ x^2+y^2=1$, the optimum occurs where the level curve of $f$ is tangent to the constraint, i.e. the gradients are parallel: $$\nabla f(x,y)=\lambda\nabla g(x,y).$$ (Solving: $2xy=2\lambda x$, $x^2=2\lambda y$, so $x^2=2y^2$, giving $y=1/\sqrt3$, $x^2=2/3$ and $f_{\max}=2/(3\sqrt3)\approx0.385$.)

Example: $\max_{x,y}xy$ subject to $x+y=6$. Lagrangian $L(x,y,\lambda)=xy-\lambda(x+y-6)$:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=y-\lambda=0,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial y}=x-\lambda=0,\quad\frac{\partial L}{\partial\lambda}=-(x+y-6)=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=y=\lambda,\ 2x=6,\ x=y=3,\ \lambda=3.$$

The values of $x,y$ are the same whether $+\lambda$ or $-\lambda$ is used for an equality constraint (only the sign of $\lambda$ flips).

sections.title: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions
sections.plain: Lagrange + inequality constraints + complementary slackness.
sections.body:
KKT generalises Lagrange multipliers (equality only) to inequality constraints. With the convention (constraints $g_i(\mathbf x)=0$, $h_j(\mathbf x)\ge0$), form

$$\mathcal L=f(\mathbf x)-\sum_i\lambda_ig_i(\mathbf x)-\sum_j\mu_jh_j(\mathbf x).$$

Necessary conditions for a minimum $\mathbf x^*$:

$$\nabla_{\mathbf x}\mathcal L(\mathbf x^*,\lambda^*,\mu^*)=0,\quad g_i(\mathbf x^*)=0,\quad h_j(\mathbf x^*)\ge0,\quad \mu_j^*\ge0,\quad \mu_j^*h_j(\mathbf x^*)=0.$$

These are stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility and complementary slackness. For convex problems with linear constraints (like the SVM) they are also sufficient. In the SVM, $h_i=y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)-1\ge0$ and $\mu_i=\alpha_i$.

sections.title: Deriving the dual
sections.plain: Eliminate w and b; maximise over α.
sections.body:
Set the derivatives of $L(\mathbf w,b,\boldsymbol\alpha)=\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2-\sum\alpha_i[y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)-1]$ to zero:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf w}=\mathbf w-\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i=0\Rightarrow\mathbf w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=-\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0\Rightarrow\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0.$$

Expand: $L=\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2-\sum\alpha_iy_i\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x_i-b\sum\alpha_iy_i+\sum\alpha_i$. Substituting both results:

$$L=\tfrac12\Big(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i\Big)\cdot\Big(\sum_j\alpha_jy_j\mathbf x_j\Big)-\Big(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i\Big)\cdot\Big(\sum_j\alpha_jy_j\mathbf x_j\Big)+\sum_i\alpha_i=\sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_i\sum_j\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\,\mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j.$$

Dual problem: maximise $W(\boldsymbol\alpha)=\sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j$ subject to $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$. It is a concave QP in $n$ variables, and the data appear only through dot products $\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j$ (the Gram matrix).

sections.title: Support vectors from KKT
sections.plain: α_i > 0 only on the margin.
sections.body: Complementary slackness: $\alpha_i[y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)-1]=0$. Either $\alpha_i=0$ and $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)-1>0$ (point strictly outside the margin), or $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)-1=0$ and $\alpha_i>0$ (point on the margin). For support vectors $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)=1$; for all other points $\alpha_i=0$. (Degenerate cases with $\alpha_i=0$ on the margin are possible but rare.)

sections.title: Solution and classification function
sections.plain: w from α; b from any SV; predict with dot products.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i\ \ (\text{learned weights }\alpha_i,\ \text{support vectors }\mathbf x_i),\qquad b=y_k-\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_k\ \text{for any support vector }k.$$ $$f(\mathbf x)=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x+b)=\operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,\mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x+b\Big).$$

If $f(\mathbf x)<0$ classify as negative, otherwise positive. Prediction relies on inner products between the test point and the support vectors; training relies on inner products between all pairs of training points. Numerically, $b$ is usually averaged over all support vectors.

sections.title: Worked example: three support vectors
sections.plain: Solve the 3×3 system; boundary x₂ = 2.
sections.body:
Data: negative points $(0,1)$, $(-1,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,-1)$; positive points $(-1,3)$, $(1,3)$, $(-1,4)$, $(1,4)$. Support vectors (circled): $\mathbf x_1=(0,1)$, $\mathbf x_2=(-1,3)$, $\mathbf x_3=(1,3)$.

Solving for α. For support vectors $f(\mathbf x)=\pm1$ exactly. Add a 1 to each vector for the bias: $\tilde{\mathbf x}_1=[0,1,1],\ y_1=-1$; $\tilde{\mathbf x}_2=[-1,3,1],\ y_2=+1$; $\tilde{\mathbf x}_3=[1,3,1],\ y_3=+1$. The system $\sum_j\alpha_jy_j\,\tilde{\mathbf x}_j\cdot\tilde{\mathbf x}_i=y_i$ is, with dot products $\tilde x_1\cdot\tilde x_1=2$, $\tilde x_1\cdot\tilde x_2=\tilde x_1\cdot\tilde x_3=4$, $\tilde x_2\cdot\tilde x_2=\tilde x_3\cdot\tilde x_3=11$, $\tilde x_2\cdot\tilde x_3=9$:

$$\begin{aligned}-2\alpha_1+4\alpha_2+4\alpha_3&=-1\\-4\alpha_1+11\alpha_2+9\alpha_3&=+1\\-4\alpha_1+9\alpha_2+11\alpha_3&=+1\end{aligned}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\alpha_1=3.5,\ \alpha_2=0.75,\ \alpha_3=0.75.$$

Solving for w and b: $\tilde{\mathbf w}=-3.5[0,1,1]+0.75[-1,3,1]+0.75[1,3,1]=[0,1,-2]$, so $\mathbf w=(0,1)$, $b=-2$. Check: $\sum\alpha_iy_i=-3.5+0.75+0.75=-2\ne0$, because this "augmented" shortcut folds $b$ into $\mathbf w$ (it solves a slightly different problem that also penalises $b$). Here the answer coincides with the true hard-margin SVM (verified in code: scikit-learn gives $\mathbf w=(0,1)$, $b=-2$, margin $2/\|\mathbf w\|=2$). With the line $ax+cy+b=0$, $\mathbf w=[a,c]$: $y=(-a/c)x+(-b/c)$, so the intercept is $-(-2)/1=2$ and the slope is $-0/1=0$.

Decision boundary: the horizontal line $x_2=2$, midway between $x_2=1$ and $x_2=3$.

sections.title: Noisy data and the case for soft margins
sections.plain: Hard margins demand zero training error.
sections.body: The hard margin requires every training point to be classified correctly, with no training error. With noisy data no separating hyperplane may exist, or the one that exists is contorted by outliers. Almost all real-world data are linearly inseparable, and even when data are separable, insisting on a perfect boundary leads to overfitting.

sections.title: Slack variables and hinge loss
sections.plain: ξᵢ = how far point i violates its margin.
sections.body:
Slack variables $\xi_i$ allow misclassification of difficult or noisy examples. There is one slack per point; $\xi_i$ is the distance of $\mathbf x_i$ from its class's margin (in units of $1/\|\mathbf w\|$) and can be read as a measure of confidence: $\xi_i=0$ beyond the margin, $0<\xi_i\le1$ inside the margin but correct, $\xi_i>1$ misclassified. Points far on the wrong side get more penalty. New criterion: minimise $\tfrac12\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf w+C\sum_{k=1}^R\xi_k$.

Hinge loss: at the optimum $\xi_i=\max\{0,1-y_i\theta^T\mathbf x_i\}$, so the problem becomes unconstrained:

$$\min_\theta\ \tfrac12\|\theta\|^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\max\{0,\,1-y^{(i)}\theta^T\mathbf x^{(i)}\}.$$

The first term maximises the margin (regularisation); the second is the cost of classifying each point. For $y=+1$ the loss is zero when $\theta^T\mathbf x\ge1$ and rises linearly below; for $y=-1$ it is zero when $\theta^T\mathbf x\le-1$. Written compactly: $\min_\mathbf w\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2+C\sum_{i=1}^N\xi_i$ subject to $y_i\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i\ge1-\xi_i,\ \xi_i\ge0$.

sections.title: Hard margin vs soft margin
sections.plain: Add C·Σξ and relax constraints to 1 − ξ.
sections.body:
Hard marginSoft margin
Objective$\tfrac12\mathbf w^T\mathbf w$$\tfrac12\mathbf w^T\mathbf w+C\sum\xi_i$
Constraints$y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1$$y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1-\xi_i,\ \xi_i\ge0$
Dual box$\alpha_i\ge0$$0\le\alpha_i\le C$
Needs separable dataYesNo

The soft-margin dual is identical to the hard-margin dual except for the upper bound $\alpha_i\le C$ (from $\partial L/\partial\xi_i=C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$, $\mu_i\ge0$). KKT then gives three groups: $\alpha_i=0$ (outside margin), $0<\alpha_i

sections.title: The C parameter: margin size vs misclassification cost
sections.plain: Large C: small margin, few training errors. Small C: wide margin.
sections.body:
$C$ tells the optimiser how much to avoid misclassifying each training example. Large $C$: chooses a smaller-margin hyperplane if it classifies more training points correctly. Very small $C$: looks for a larger-margin hyperplane even if it misclassifies more points.

The training-set illustration: low $C$ ("misclassification ok, want large margin") tilts the line and leaves one blue point misclassified; large $C$ ("misclassification not ok") moves the line to classify it, shrinking the margin. On test set Aand test set B, the large-margin low-$C$ boundary generalises better on one and the large-$C$ boundary on the other: which is right depends on whether that outlier was noise or signal, so choose $C$ by validation. Equivalent view: $C\approx1/\lambda$ in "hinge loss + $\lambda\|\mathbf w\|^2$".

sections.title: Non-linear SVMs and feature spaces
sections.plain: Map to a space where the data are linearly separable.
sections.body: Part II topics: non-linear SVM, kernel trick, SVM kernels, multi-class problem, applications. Data separable with some noise are handled well by the soft margin. If the data are too hard, e.g. 1-D points with one class in the middle, map $x\to(x,x^2)$: in 2-D a line separates them. General idea: the original input space can be mapped to a higher-dimensional feature space where the training set is separable, $\Phi:\mathbf x\to\phi(\mathbf x)$ (a circle-separated dataset becomes plane-separated in 3-D).

sections.title: Overlapping classes: transformation and the dual in feature space
sections.plain: Linear SVM on φ(x); boundary w·φ(x) + b = 0.
sections.body:
When the data are not linearly separable the margin becomes inefficient; transform from $\mathbf x$ to $\Phi(\mathbf x)$ so a linear boundary applies. Example: $$\Phi:(x_1,x_2)\longrightarrow(x_1^2,\ x_2^2,\ \sqrt2x_1,\ \sqrt2x_2,\ 1),$$ choose $\mathbf w=(w_0,\dots,w_4)$ with $w_4x_1^2+w_3x_2^2+w_2\sqrt2x_1+w_1\sqrt2x_2+w_0=0$, a conic (circle/ellipse) in the original space; in general $\mathbf w\cdot\Phi(\mathbf x)+b=0$.

Steps: (1) transform the input into a higher-dimensional space with a non-linear mapping; (2) search for a linear separating hyperplane there. This is again the linear-SVM QP; the maximum-margin hyperplane in the new space is a non-linear hypersurface in the original space.

Learning: non-overlapping case $\min\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2+C\sum\xi_i$ s.t. $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1-\xi_i$; non-linear case replaces $\mathbf x_i$ by $\phi(\mathbf x_i)$. Dual: $$\max_\lambda\sum_i\lambda_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_jy_iy_j\,\phi(\mathbf x_i)\cdot\phi(\mathbf x_j)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \sum\lambda_iy_i=0,\ \lambda_i\ge0,$$ then $\mathbf w=\sum\lambda_iy_i\phi(\mathbf x_i)$ and $\lambda_i\{y_i(\sum_j\lambda_jy_j\phi(\mathbf x_j)\cdot\phi(\mathbf x_i)+b)-1\}=0$ gives $b$. A test instance $\mathbf z$ is classified by $$f(\mathbf z)=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf w\cdot\phi(\mathbf z)+b)=\operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iy_i\,\phi(\mathbf x_i)\cdot\phi(\mathbf z)+b\Big).$$ The only missing piece is computing $\phi(\mathbf x_i)\cdot\phi(\mathbf z)$ efficiently: the kernel trick.

sections.title: Kernels and the kernel trick
sections.plain: Compute φ(x)·φ(z) without computing φ.
sections.body: Kernel functions compute the relationship between every pair of points as if they were in high dimension, without actually transforming the data. This avoids the cost of the transformation. A kernel is a function corresponding to an inner product in some expanded feature space: $$K(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=\phi(\mathbf x_i)^T\phi(\mathbf x_j).$$ In the hypothesis $h_\theta(\mathbf x)=\theta_0+\sum_i\alpha_iy^{(i)}\mathbf x^T\mathbf x^{(i)}$, replace the dot product by $k(\mathbf x,\mathbf x^{(i)})=\Phi(\mathbf x)^T\Phi(\mathbf x^{(i)})$: the same form, without ever knowing $\Phi$. Cost: a kernel evaluation is $O(d)$ while the explicit map can be $O(d^p)$ or infinite-dimensional (RBF).

sections.title: Common kernel functions
sections.plain: Linear, polynomial, Gaussian (RBF), sigmoid.
sections.body:
$$\text{Linear: }K(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j\qquad\text{Polynomial of power }p:\ K=(1+\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j)^p$$ $$\text{Gaussian (RBF): }K=\exp\Big(-\frac{\|\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\qquad\text{Sigmoid: }K=\tanh(\beta_0\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j+\beta_1)$$

Notes: the RBF feature space is infinite-dimensional; small $\sigma$ (large $\gamma=1/2\sigma^2$) gives very local, wiggly boundaries. The sigmoid kernel is positive semi-definite only for some $\beta_0,\beta_1$, so it is not always a valid Mercer kernel.

sections.title: Polynomial kernel examples
sections.plain: (a·b)² and (1 + x·z)² equal explicit dot products.
sections.body:
Degree-2, 2-D: with $\phi(\mathbf a)=(a_1^2,\sqrt2a_1a_2,a_2^2)$,

$$\phi(\mathbf a)^T\phi(\mathbf b)=a_1^2b_1^2+2a_1b_1a_2b_2+a_2^2b_2^2=(a_1b_1+a_2b_2)^2=(\mathbf a^T\mathbf b)^2.$$

3-D to 9-D: $\phi(\mathbf x)=(x_1^2,x_1x_2,x_1x_3,x_2x_1,x_2^2,x_2x_3,x_3x_1,x_3x_2,x_3^2)^T$, so $\phi(\mathbf x)^T\phi(\mathbf y)=\sum_{i,j=1}^3x_ix_jy_iy_j=(\mathbf x^T\mathbf y)^2$. The kernel needs 3 multiplications and a square instead of building two 9-vectors.

Is $(1+\mathbf x^{(i)T}\mathbf x^{(j)})^2$ a kernel?Expand: $$1+x_1^{(i)2}x_1^{(j)2}+2x_1^{(i)}x_1^{(j)}x_2^{(i)}x_2^{(j)}+x_2^{(i)2}x_2^{(j)2}+2x_1^{(i)}x_1^{(j)}+2x_2^{(i)}x_2^{(j)}=\Phi(\mathbf x^{(i)})^T\Phi(\mathbf x^{(j)})$$ with $\Phi(\mathbf x)=(1,x_1^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2,x_2^2,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2)$. So yes.

sections.title: Mercer kernels and constructing kernels
sections.plain: Symmetric, PSD; closed under +, ×, positive scaling.
sections.body:
Which functions correspond to feature vectors $\phi(\mathbf x)$? Mercer kernels: $K$ is continuous; symmetric, $K(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=\phi(\mathbf x_i)^T\phi(\mathbf x_j)=\phi(\mathbf x_j)^T\phi(\mathbf x_i)=K(\mathbf x_j,\mathbf x_i)$; and positive semi-definite: every Gram matrix $\mathbf K$ satisfies $\mathbf c^T\mathbf K\mathbf c\ge0$ for all $\mathbf c$. PSD ensures the dual is a concave maximisation (single global optimum).

Constructing kernels: (1) from scratch: any $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^m$ gives $k(x,x')=\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(x')\rangle$; and if $d$ is a distance function (non-negative, zero only for $x=x'$, symmetric, triangle inequality) then $k(x,x')=\exp(-d(x,x'))$ is stated to be a kernel. (2) From other kernels: if $k$ is a kernel and $\alpha>0$, $\alpha k$ and $k+\alpha$ are kernels; if $k_1,k_2$ are kernels, $k_1+k_2$ and $k_1\cdot k_2$ are kernels.

sections.title: Kernelised dual and hypothesis
sections.plain: Replace every ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩ by K(xᵢ, xⱼ).
sections.body:
$$\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}W(\boldsymbol\alpha)=\sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\,K(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)\quad\text{s.t.}\ \alpha_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0,$$ $$f(\mathbf x)=\operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_i\alpha_iy_iK(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x)+b\Big).$$

For example, the polynomial kernel with $d=4$ including lower-order terms is $(\langle\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j\rangle+1)^4$: "these are kernels, so by the kernel trick we just replace them".

sections.title: Worked Example-1: a non-linear SVM
sections.plain: Map, pick 3 SVs, solve, read off x₁ + x₂ ≈ 10.
sections.body:
Data: blue $(1,1),(-1,1),(-1,-1),(1,-1)$; red $(2,0),(0,2),(-2,0),(0,-2)$. No separating line exists. Mapping:

$$\Phi\binom{x_1}{x_2}=\begin{cases}\binom{6-x_1+(x_1-x_2)^2}{6-x_2+(x_1-x_2)^2}&\text{if }\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}\ge2\\[4pt]\binom{x_1}{x_2}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Blue vectors are unchanged since $\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}<2$. Red: $(2,0)\to(8,10)$, $(0,2)\to(10,8)$, $(-2,0)\to(12,10)$, $(0,-2)\to(10,12)$. Choose support vectors $S_1=(8,10)$, $S_2=(10,8)$, $S_3=(1,1)$ and augment with a bias 1: $\tilde S_1=(8,10,1)$, $\tilde S_2=(10,8,1)$, $\tilde S_3=(1,1,1)$. Equations, with the positive class red:

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha_1\tilde S_1\!\cdot\!\tilde S_1+\alpha_2\tilde S_2\!\cdot\!\tilde S_1-\alpha_3\tilde S_3\!\cdot\!\tilde S_1&=+1&\Rightarrow\ 165\alpha_1+161\alpha_2-19\alpha_3&=+1\\ \alpha_1\tilde S_1\!\cdot\!\tilde S_2+\alpha_2\tilde S_2\!\cdot\!\tilde S_2-\alpha_3\tilde S_3\!\cdot\!\tilde S_2&=+1&\Rightarrow\ 161\alpha_1+165\alpha_2-19\alpha_3&=+1\\ \alpha_1\tilde S_1\!\cdot\!\tilde S_3+\alpha_2\tilde S_2\!\cdot\!\tilde S_3-\alpha_3\tilde S_3\!\cdot\!\tilde S_3&=-1&\Rightarrow\ 19\alpha_1+19\alpha_2-3\alpha_3&=-1\end{aligned}$$

Solution: $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0.0859$, $\alpha_3=1.4219$ (a commonly quoted version prints 0.859). Then $$\tilde{\mathbf w}=0.0859\begin{pmatrix}8\\10\\1\end{pmatrix}+0.0859\begin{pmatrix}10\\8\\1\end{pmatrix}-1.4219\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.1243\\0.1243\\-1.2501\end{pmatrix}.$$ The boundary $0.1243x_1+0.1243x_2-1.2501=0$; dividing by 0.1243: $\mathbf w=(1,1)$, offset $b=-1.2501/0.1243=-10.057$, i.e. $x_1+x_2=10.057$ (exactly $10$ with unrounded α: $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=11/128$, $\alpha_3=91/64$, $\tilde{\mathbf w}=(1/8,1/8,-5/4)$). This is the decision surface in feature space; in input space it is non-linear.

sections.title: Non-linear SVM using kernels: steps
sections.plain: Kernel → Gram matrix → QP → predict with kernels.
sections.body:
1. Select a kernel function.
  2. Compute pairwise kernel values between labelled examples (the kernel/Gram matrix).
  3. Use the kernel matrix to solve for the support vectors and α weights (QP).
  4. To classify a new example: compute kernel values between it and the support vectors, apply the α weights, and check the sign of $\sum\alpha_iy_iK(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x)+b$.
TRAIN(X, y, K, C):
  G[i][j] ← K(x_i, x_j)  for all i, j               // O(n² d)
  α ← argmax Σα − ½ ΣΣ α_i α_j y_i y_j G[i][j]
       s.t. 0 ≤ α_i ≤ C, Σ α_i y_i = 0              // QP / SMO, ~O(n²)–O(n³)
  SV ← { i : α_i > ε }
  b ← mean over i with 0 < α_i < C of ( y_i − Σ_j α_j y_j G[j][i] )
PREDICT(x): return sign( Σ_{i∈SV} α_i y_i K(x_i, x) + b )   // O(|SV| d)

sections.title: SVM versus logistic regression
sections.plain: Hinge loss vs log-loss, same regulariser.
sections.body:
As regularised empirical loss minimisation:

$$\text{SVM: }\sum_{i=1}^n\big(1-y_i[w_0+\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf w_1]\big)^++\|\mathbf w_1\|^2/2,\qquad \text{Logistic: }\sum_{i=1}^n-\log\sigma\big(y_i[w_0+\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf w_1]\big)+\|\mathbf w_1\|^2/2,$$

with $\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$ ($-\log\sigma=-\log P(y_i|\mathbf x,\mathbf w)$; maximising penalised log-likelihood became minimising penalised negative log-likelihood). The difference is how errors are penalised, as a function of $z=y_i[w_0+\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf w_1]$: SVM $\text{Loss}(z)=(1-z)^+$; regularised logistic $\text{Loss}(z)=\log(1+\exp(-z))$.

Interpretation: LR maximises the probability of the data; the farther a point lies on the correct side, the happier LR is. The SVM maximises the distance of the closest points (support vectors); a point that is not a support vector doesn't matter. Consequences: LR gives calibrated probabilities and all points influence it; SVM is sparse and more robust to well-classified points, but needs calibration for probabilities.

sections.title: Properties of SVMs
sections.plain: Flexible, sparse, dimension-independent, controllable, convex.
sections.body:
• Flexibility in choosing a similarity function (kernel).
  • Sparseness of solution with large datasets: only support vectors specify the hyperplane, so SVMs are called sparse kernel machines.
  • Ability to handle large feature spaces: complexity does not depend on the dimensionality of the feature space.
  • Overfitting can be controlled by the soft-margin approach.
  • A simple convex optimisation problem guaranteed to converge to a single global solution.

sections.title: Pros and cons
sections.plain: Powerful and compact; kernel choice and O(n²) cost.
sections.body: Pros: the kernel framework is powerful and flexible; often a sparse set of support vectors (compact at test time); works very well in practice, even with small training sets; the solution is a quadratic program. Cons: selecting the best kernel can be tricky; computation and memory: kernel values must be computed for all pairs of training examples ($O(n^2)$ memory), and learning can take a very long time for large-scale problems (roughly $O(n^2)$ to $O(n^3)$ time).

sections.title: Multi-class SVMs
sections.plain: One-vs-all (C models) or one-vs-one (C(C − 1)/2 models).
sections.body:
With $C$ classes, e.g. predicting which movie genre a viewer likes best (action, drama, indie, thriller, …), two approaches:

One-vs-all: train $C$ classifiers; in each, positives are class $i$ and negatives all other classes; the class with the most confident prediction wins. Example with 4 classes: scores 3.5, 6.2, 1.4, 5.5 → final prediction class 2. Issues: the scores of separately trained SVMs are not on a common scale, and each problem is imbalanced (1 class vs $C-1$).

One-vs-one: train $C(C-1)/2$ binary classifiers, one per pair; all vote. With 4 classes, 6 classifiers 1v2, 1v3, 1v4, 2v3, 2v4, 3v4 with votes 1, 1, 4, 2, 4, 4: class 4 gets 3 votes, class 1 gets 2, class 2 gets 1 → class 4. Each model trains on less data (faster per model for SVMs); scikit-learn's SVC uses one-vs-one internally.

Boundarylinearany (kernel)lineararbitrary
  • "More support vectors means a better model." Usually the opposite: many SVs often indicate overlap or too small C; the leave-one-out error is bounded by #SV/n.
  • "RBF is always best." For high-dimensional sparse data (text) the linear kernel is often as good and far faster.
  • "b can be ignored." Folding b into w (augmented vectors, as in the shortcut) regularises b too; standard SVMs leave b unpenalised.
  • "Hinge loss is differentiable." It is not at z = 1; use subgradients or the QP.

code.title: Hard-margin SVM by hand: both reference examples
code.explain: Solves the 3×3 systems for α in the linear example and the non-linear Example-1, and recovers w and b.
mistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the labels yᵢ when forming the equations.
code.notes: Exact fractions show that the Example-1 boundary is x₁ + x₂ = 10; the −10.057 comes from rounding.
code.code:
import numpy as np

# Example: support vectors augmented with a bias input of 1
S = np.array([[0, 1, 1], [-1, 3, 1], [1, 3, 1]], float); y = np.array([-1, 1, 1], float)
G = (S * y[:, None]) @ S.T                     # entry (i, j) = y_j * x_j . x_i   (convention)
A = (S @ S.T) * y[None, :]                     # sum_j alpha_j y_j x_j . x_i = y_i
alpha = np.linalg.solve(A, y)
w_aug = (alpha * y) @ S
print("equations:\n", A); print("alpha =", alpha.round(3)); print("w_aug =", w_aug.round(3), "-> w =", w_aug[:2], "b =", w_aug[2])

# Example-1: nonlinear map, then the same procedure
phi = lambda x: np.array([6 - x[0] + (x[0] - x[1]) ** 2, 6 - x[1] + (x[0] - x[1]) ** 2]) if np.hypot(*x) >= 2 else np.array(x, float)
for r in [(2, 0), (0, 2), (-2, 0), (0, -2)]: print("phi", r, "=", phi(r))
S = np.array([[8, 10, 1], [10, 8, 1], [1, 1, 1]], float); y = np.array([1, 1, -1], float)
M = S @ S.T; print("dot products:\n", M)
a = np.linalg.solve(M * y[None, :], y)                 # signed alphas: alpha_j * y_j appear in the system
print("alpha =", a.round(4))
w = (a * y) @ S; print("w_aug =", w.round(4), " normalised w =", (w[:2] / w[0]).round(3), " b =", round(w[2] / w[0], 3))

code.title: scikit-learn SVC: hard margin check, kernels and C
code.explain: Confirms w = (0, 1), b = −2 for the first example, then compares linear, polynomial and RBF kernels on circular data and shows how the number of support vectors falls as C rises.
mistakes: Not scaling features before an RBF SVM.
code.notes: Use SVC(probability=True) or CalibratedClassifierCV when probabilities are needed.
code.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# Linear hard-margin check on the 6 points (large C approximates hard margin)
X = np.array([[0, 1], [-1, 3], [1, 3], [-1, 0], [1, 0], [0, -1], [-1, 4], [1, 4]], float)
y = np.array([-1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1, 1, 1])
m = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(X, y)
print("w =", m.coef_.round(3), "b =", m.intercept_.round(3), "support vectors:", m.support_vectors_.tolist())

# Effect of C and kernel on non-linear data
X, y = make_circles(400, noise=0.12, factor=0.4, random_state=0)
for k in ["linear", "poly", "rbf"]:
    for C in [0.1, 10]:
        s = cross_val_score(SVC(kernel=k, degree=2, C=C, gamma="scale"), X, y, cv=5).mean()
        n = SVC(kernel=k, degree=2, C=C, gamma="scale").fit(X, y).n_support_.sum()
        print(f"{k:6s} C={C:<4} CV acc {s:.3f}  #SV {n}")
